concept.name: Insider trading
concept.definition: Illegal insider trading refers generally to buying or selling a security, in breach of a fiduciary duty or other relationship of trust and confidence, on the basis of material, nonpublic information about the security. Not all trading by corporate insiders is illegal: insiders may lawfully trade when they do so without using material nonpublic information and report their transactions as required.
concept.intuition: If you trade using secret, market-moving information that you were entrusted with and weren't supposed to use, you're stealing an unfair edge from everyone on the other side of your trade.
concept.mechanics: Liability under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 requires (1) material nonpublic information, (2) a breach of duty by the insider who trades or tips, and (3) scienter. Tippers and tippees can both be liable; a tippee is liable when trading on the tip while knowing the tipper breached a duty and received a personal benefit.
concept.failure_modes: Materiality and breach-of-duty are fact-specific, making borderline cases (mosaic research, expert networks, political intelligence) hard to classify; lawful Rule 10b5-1 plans can be abused by adopting them while aware of MNPI, undermining their affirmative defense.
concept.misconceptions: Insider trading is not any trading by an insider — insiders trade legally all the time with proper disclosure; nor is trading on a hot rumor automatically illegal — the trader must be in or downstream of a breached duty of trust or confidence.
concept.example: A CFO learns privately that quarterly earnings will badly miss estimates and sells 20,000 shares two days before the announcement, avoiding a 30% loss; the SEC charges her under Rule 10b-5.

citations.source: Investor.gov Glossary (SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy)
